claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the as-cast single-phase solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
This CoCrFeNiTi state has favorable ductility, plasticity, and machinability.
High chemical homogeneity in the starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy minimizes chemical short-range order and nanoscale precipitate formation.
The absence of localized compositional modulations permits relatively unimpeded dislocation glide.
Relatively easy dislocation glide causes the starting alloy's low yield strength and hardness.
Chemical short-range order or nanoscale element-rich precipitates act as dislocation-pinning obstacles.
Microstructural or phase-state changes can govern the hardness and strength of high-entropy alloys.
Dislocation-pinning obstacles increase the energy barrier for dislocation motion, thereby increasing yield strength and hardness while reducing ductility.
Annealing CoCrFeNiTi at approximately 600–700 °C followed by rapid cooling will induce incipient chemical ordering or nanoscale precipitates.
The treatment should increase hardness and yield strength by roughly 20–30% or more relative to the as-cast alloy.
The treatment should moderately reduce plastic strain relative to the as-cast alloy.
Local ordering or nanoscale precipitates should be detectable after treatment and correlate with enhanced hardness and strength.
The proposed mechanism is limited to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi initially in a single-phase state and tested at room temperature under conventional strain rates.
Formation of additional phases or processing outside the recommended temperature and time window may alter or overshadow the proposed strengthening mechanism.
Failure to obtain at least a 10–20% increase in both hardness and yield strength, despite evidence of increased ordering or nanoprecipitation and pinning, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Nanoscale precipitate formation is presented as a central mediator of strengthening, but the boundary states that development of additional phases may alter or overshadow the mechanism. Because precipitates ordinarily constitute an additional phase, the stated applicability boundary is inconsistent with one branch of the proposed mechanism.
